sentences.t: Wylie Capital wants to turn the Merrillville Commerce Center at Broadway, 93rd Avenue and Georgia Street into a data center site of up to six buildings, in Merrillville, in Lake County, Indiana.
The Chicago firm's plan runs to 1.2 million square feet and up to $600 million, with as many as 200 jobs, most of them paying six figures.
The buildings would stand up to three storeys, two of them in a first phase, and Merrillville's data center advisory committee gave the plan preliminary approval in November 2024.

Two more proposals arrived alongside it: Province Group's, up to $500 million and a million square feet in the Merrillville Technology Park near Colorado Street and Harms Road, and Karis Critical's, on 180 acres on 101st Avenue east of Deep River County Park at up to $900 million.

Town council president Rick Bella called the prospect "a huge boon to the tax base of course once these buildings are totally finished and operational", and a thousand homes were already going up at Liberty Estates for the workers the town expected.
Then the council stopped.

At its meeting on the Tuesday night of 26 May 2026 it placed a moratorium on data center projects, running from 1 June to 31 May 2027, to assess what one would do to infrastructure, utilities, traffic, noise, economic development, tax revenue and neighbourhood compatibility.
The motion was proposed by councilman Shawn Pettit, it passed unanimously, and some of the residents in the audience stood and clapped.
Four developers had approached the town by then, and one proposal had advanced further than the others; the town did not say which.

Bella told the meeting that watching how things had gone in Hobart, where officials have sparred with residents over environmental, quality of life and traffic impacts, "may ultimately provide Merrillville leaders with valuable information necessary to make a more informed and educated decision for our residents and our future".
Residents came to the podium on both sides of it.

Jennifer Gross handed over paper copies of what she said were Harvard University studies on the effects of data centers, and said they showed communities needed to "open their eyes" to what the industry was doing to municipalities.
A resident who did not give his name said he had polled a Merrillville Facebook group on whether to build one: 280 voted against, 11 for and eight were undecided.

Another said he was disappointed, that "no one was crying" when factories and warehouses went up elsewhere in Lake County, and that "we need to rethink this and rethink about taking opportunity when opportunity comes knocking", because, he said, "opportunity doesn't usually knock twice".
What Hobart is building is Amazon's, agreed with the city a day after the company announced $15 billion for campuses in northern Indiana in November 2025.

Mayor Josh Huddlestun said it would bring thousands of construction jobs and close to a thousand long term ones, that Amazon would fully fund the infrastructure work, and that NIPSCO's subsidiary GenCo would cover its energy needs and any new power infrastructure.

The Northwest Indiana Forum was booked to put expert speakers in front of Merrillville residents at the Dean and Barbara White Community Center on 6600 Broadway at half past five on 11 June 2026, with breakout sessions for questions.

Pettit, who moved the moratorium, said he liked the prospect of the property tax a data center would pay and thought the town should look at other ways of easing its budget first, but that the decision was not really his to argue with: "If they don't want it, they don't want it. I'm not going to try and convince them from a financial standpoint. I don't know that's necessarily our job. We just need to listen to residents."

unconfirmed:
The record gives the address as Crown Point (46307), while every report places the Wylie Capital site in Merrillville; the two towns adjoin. No megawatt figure, acreage, water demand, filing date or plan commission action on the Wylie Capital project has been published, and the town's moratorium page does not say which of the four proposals had advanced furthest. Whether the June 11, 2026 education meeting took place as scheduled was not checked, and nothing published since May 2026 says what has become of the Wylie Capital plan under the moratorium.

Correction, made after this page was first published. The first version sourced the moratorium from a press release and from Northwest Indiana Business Magazine's write-up of it, and its note said the Times of Northwest Indiana "serves its article text scrambled to non-subscribers". That was wrong. The kAm markers in the page are the BLOX/TownNews template, not a paywall, and the article is served to anyone who requests it; decoding it requires unescaping HTML entities before applying ROT47, because ROT47 of the letter m is a character the page must ship as an entity. Decoded, Lizzie Kaboski's report of the meeting carries what the release did not: who moved the motion, that it passed unanimously, that residents stood and clapped, and four residents speaking for and against. The page is now written from that report and the press-release wording has been dropped where the reporter covered the same ground.

sentences.t: On 20 January 2026 the Clinton County commissioners unanimously refused to rezone 715 acres of farmland north of Frankfort for a data center campus proposed by Logix Realty.
Logix Realty is an affiliate of the developer Logistix, whose president, Doug Swain, had said the project would bring more than $10 billion of investment.

Swain laid out the plan on 15 July 2025 to about 30 landowners and others in the Chamber of Commerce meeting room in the Iron Block Building: more than 700 acres north of the Conagra plant, up to 7 million square feet in several buildings, as much as 600 megawatts, and a buyer to be found among well capitalized firms such as Meta or Amazon, with everyone involved under a nondisclosure agreement.

Asked about water, he said newer data centers use less and some are air cooled; asked about noise, he compared it to road traffic; asked where residents could see something similar, he said "you may have to at least go to Ohio".
He put the jobs at half a job per megawatt, about 300, paying around $100,000 a year, and said of the tax effect: "we are studying that right now".

The first application, filed by Logix Realty on 3 July 2025, asked Frankfort to rezone 833 acres from agriculture to general business and bring the land inside the city, and was due before the city plan commission on 23 July.

Mayor Judith Sheets put out a statement on the "frustration, fear, and anger circulating throughout our community regarding the proposed data center project", and Logistix rescinded the request, saying it would go to the county instead.
The county commissioners said at the time that they were "not for or against the proposal at this time" and needed more information.

In early September 2025 Logistix brought the county area plan commission a smaller plan, the Logix I campus on 155 acres across the railroad from the Conagra plant, with about 170 jobs and $1 billion of investment.

More than 100 people came, more than a dozen spoke about noise, light and water, and Kevin Myers, a plan commission member who is also a county commissioner, said: "There's too many unanswered questions that I don't feel like I could be in favor of anything but a negative recommendation."

The board deadlocked and sent the request on with no recommendation, after member Jeff Chynoweth, the one vote against a negative recommendation, was booed for saying some people would say no to anything on that land.

On 18 November 2025, before the commissioners voted, Logix withdrew it; the area plan director, Liz Stitzel, said a revised filing would follow and could grow to about 1,200 acres with a casting company involved.

The new petition covered 714.55 acres in Washington and Union townships, named DataOne as the intended user, and described a three part campus: a data center, a precast concrete plant and a hydroponic "gigafarm".

At the 6 January 2026 hearing supporters put the first investment at $10 billion to $12 billion, rising possibly to $50 billion, and neighbors raised aquifer depletion, noise and the loss of farmland.

The developer agreed in principle to 14 binding commitments, among them a 65 decibel limit at the property line, closed loop water and a decommissioning plan backed by financial security, and Stitzel told the board: "Staff would strongly caution against any favorable recommendation without a full set of clear commitments."
The commission voted to send a favorable recommendation.
Two weeks later commissioners Bert Weaver, Kevin Myers and Jordan Brewer turned it down.
Myers said: "Given what this has put our community through and given that the majority of our residents are against this project, I cannot support the rezone."

Weaver said the project "could be a tremendous boost" but that he had grown "uncomfortable" with the negotiations, and Brewer said: "We want development, but we want to work with partners we trust on projects that are economically beneficial to the community as a whole."

Weaver also objected that the developer had offered to pay for only half of the road in front of the entrance, which he called a red flag, and reportedly said it wanted to "nickel and dime" the county.
The denial bars the same request for 12 months.
Inside the city, the Frankfort Board of Zoning Appeals had granted Logix a variance for a data center on land east of Conagra on 23 April 2025.

On 2 February 2026 Mayor Sheets set conditions for any DataOne proposal in the city industrial park, including public town halls and published economic and environmental impact studies, saying: "Our community deserves facts and not assumptions when evaluating a project of this magnitude."

In September 2026 DataOne asked the city to approve a $7.5 billion "AI factory" on 115 acres of the Logix Innovation Campus, land already zoned for light industry, with an 800,000 square foot building and about 200 permanent jobs.

Its chief executive, Charles-Antoine Beyney, promised closed loop cooling using about 22,000 gallons a day, on-site fuel cells and no diesel generators, and two new substations paid for by the company, and named the chief complaints at its Vineland, New Jersey campus as "Lack of communication, number one by far," followed by noise.
At the company's open house on 21 September 2026, electrical engineer Kevin Thomas put the draw at 350 megawatts from the grid through IMPA plus 175 megawatts from Bloom Energy gas fuel cells.

The city's financial adviser, Gary Smith of Reedy Financial Group, projected about $331 million for Frankfort through 2054, against a shortfall of $4.3 million to $4.5 million in 2030 from state tax changes that could otherwise cost about 40 city jobs.
Deborah Pearson, a county council candidate from Center Township, said she was "adamantly opposed", and a masked protester outside called data centers "a cancer in the community".
Sheets, who votes only to break a tie, said "This is not a perfect project," and "There is no perfect project."
Council members are holding listening sessions at the Chamber of Commerce from 23 to 25 September.
The council is expected to take up the proposal at a special meeting on 28 September 2026.
Councilman Steve Beardsley said: "We want your voices to be heard and look forward to some fruitful conversations."

unconfirmed: The record lists 300 megawatts on 833 acres; the 833 acres and 300 megawatts are the July 2025 city filing as reported by DCD, while Doug Swain told landowners the same month the campus could draw as much as 600 megawatts, and the county petition of January 2026 was 714.55 acres. Swain pitched the project under Logistix Property Group; DCD and Inside INdiana Business call the developer Logistix, Cincinnati based, with Logix Realty as the applying affiliate. The WTHR report (403) and the Fox59 report (403) were not read; WISH-TV, Clinton County Today, Clinton County Daily News and DCD carry the same January 20 2026 vote. The 155 acre September 2025 request was due before commissioners on September 16 2025; what happened between then and the November 18 withdrawal was not found. The quotation "Our community deserves facts..." is from Clinton County Today paraphrasing a written statement; the full statement is a city PDF not read. Whether DataOne's 115 acre city site is the land covered by the April 23 2025 variance is not stated in anything read. Searches run: "Logistix data center Frankfort Indiana Clinton County commissioners", "Clinton County Indiana data center 2026", "Frankfort City Council listening sessions proposed data center", "Supporters Cite $331 Million data center Frankfort", "Logix Realty Frankfort data center September 2025 commissioners vote 155 acres". The council vote of September 28 2026 had not happened when this was written.

sentences.t: Jumping Bison LLC plans a data center in a 550 acre Economic Revitalization Area at Greensburg, in Decatur County, which takes in the Business Enterprise Park along Interstate 74 across from Honda's Indiana Auto Plant.

At the Greensburg City Council meeting of 10 December 2024 the public hearing on the company's abatement drew no comment, and the council approved a ten year, 60 percent abatement on its real property tax.
The motion creating the Economic Revitalization Area and granting the abatement passed 7 to 0.

Bryan Robbins of the Greensburg/Decatur County Economic Development Corporation brought the request, with the lawyers Rick Hall and Matt Ehinger there to answer questions; Ehinger said the multi-building campus, on about 340 acres north of town, would be built in two phases of $400 million each.
The number of jobs was not given.

The company agreed to pay all staff 125 percent of the Decatur County average wage and to make a yearly economic development payment of $1.3 million per building, under the state law that lets data centers investing more than $400 million and creating 20 jobs at an average of $40,000 receive abatements for up to 30 years.
Robbins said: "We're excited that the city council is supportive and there have been a lot of people who have contributed to this, and get this far, and we look forward to keeping it moving."
Who stands behind Jumping Bison has never been made public; the county has said only that it is a US company.

In September 2025 residents organized as the Coalition to Protect Decatur County and started a Change.org petition to the city council that reads: "We deserve to have a vote in this and our voices should be heard."
It had more than 950 signatures by the end of October 2025.

At its second meeting, on 1 November 2025, the coalition's concern was water: the city's water plant, built in 2021, is rated at 5.5 million gallons a day, and 828 million gallons went through the treatment plant the previous year, about 2.3 million a day.

The coalition cites a 1970s EPA study putting the Downeyville aquifer, which also serves Rush, Henry, Shelby and Bartholomew counties, at about 3 million gallons a day, and says the city already draws from the Flatrock River when permitted.

In its own tally of county land sales it lists eight parcels, from 36 to 119 acres, sold to Jumping Bison for a total of $43 million, which it compares to Indiana farmland at $10,000 to $15,000 an acre, with about 94 acres more not yet sold.
It also reports that the company's engineers told City Hall on 3 September 2025 that engineering for the project, which it calls "Popcorn", was about 60 percent complete.
By September 2026 the petition had 2,594 verified signatures.

unconfirmed: Acreage conflicts: WRBI and DCD give 550 acres for the Economic Revitalization Area and the campus, the Greensburg Daily News report (read via Yahoo) says the data center would take about 340 acres, and the Coalition's own list of land sales totals about 454 acres. The "Popcorn" code name, the $43 million of land purchases and the 60 percent engineering figure come only from the Coalition's Substack, not from a news outlet or public record, and are attributed accordingly. The record's $800 million figure is the two $400 million phases. No megawatt figure, water demand, filing or construction date has been published, and no report after November 2025 was found on whether the project is moving; the Baxtel listing calls it "In Doubt" without a date. The annexation "earlier this year" in WRBI is dated to 2024 by the December 2024 meeting date. The Change.org start date (September 5 2025) is from the page's metadata. Searches run: "Jumping Bison data center Greensburg Decatur County", "Decatur County Indiana data center 2026 coalition"; the Coalition's Substack archive was read in full (five posts, November 2025).

sentences.t: Project Redline is the code name the Indiana Economic Development Corporation used on 25 June 2025 for a hyperscale data center in Hancock County, Indiana, whose owner it would not name.
The unidentified end user pledged 50 jobs and $1 billion of investment by 2029, and the agency's business development committee approved a tax break it valued at $42 million over an initial 35 years.

The break, created by the legislature in 2019, exempts a data center from sales tax on its servers and other equipment and from utility tax on the electricity that runs them, and can be renewed for three further five year periods with more investment.
Redline was one of four approved that day, with Project Louie in Morgan County, Project Flo in Marion County and Project Maize in LaPorte County, $168 million in all.
Agency spokeswoman Erin Sweitzer declined to name the companies and said it could not confirm whether the projects were ones already reported.
The Hancock County project in the news in the months before had been proposed by Surge Development of Shelbyville, which withdrew its rezoning request in May 2025 after significant public opposition.

That was a 775 acre MegaSite in Buck Creek Township, around 3400 West 500 North just east of the Indianapolis Regional Airport, and the only data center images in its filings were of Google facilities.
Opposition centred on Tuttle Orchards next door, and Surge said it would focus "on working directly with the specific users who have expressed interest in the site."
Surge's principal, Chris King, sits on the agency's board and recused himself before the data centers came up, so he did not vote on Redline.
Data Center Dynamics wrote that Project Redline "likely refers" to the Surge site.

Hancock County's commissioners answered by building a gate: on 16 June 2026 they passed an ordinance, unanimously and effective at once, limiting data centers to land zoned industrial general, creating a data center overlay district and giving themselves the final vote on any project.

A developer must now write to the commissioners first, and they decide whether the project promotes public health, safety and welfare, fits the comprehensive plan and the character of the industrial general district, is the most desirable use of the land, conserves property values in the district and counts as responsible development.
Only then does it reach a technical review, a plan commission public hearing and a final commissioners' vote.

County planning director Kayla Brooks said the old definition had lumped data centers in with "communication service exchange" and made them a permitted use in several districts: "Before, they could just go to the Board of Zoning Appeals and get it approved without coming to (the commissioners)."

Commissioner Gary McDaniel said afterwards that an overlay was chosen over a moratorium because a pause would tie the county's hands, and that two data center companies were looking at Hancock County without having approached the commissioners.
A citizens committee on data center siting is to report to the plan commission by the end of 2026 with the development standards the ordinance does not yet carry.

unconfirmed: Not confirmed: whether Project Redline is the Surge Development MegaSite. The Indiana Economic Development Corporation would not say; Data Center Dynamics's link is its own inference, and the Daily Journal notes only that Surge had proposed a Hancock County project and withdrawn it. The developer, the exact site, the acreage, the megawatts and the current status of Redline are not public, and the county says no data center company has yet approached the commissioners. The record gives the town as Greenfield (46140) by postal code only. Searches this pass: 'Hancock County Indiana data center zoning ordinance June 2026 Greenfield commissioners Surge MegaSite'. The overlay ordinance, which earlier stood on this page as an unsourced background line, is now read in the Greenfield Daily Reporter; the county's citizens advisory committee minutes on hancockin.gov were not opened.

sentences.t: Eagle Creek Township has about 1,700 people in it, and the proposal is for 500 megawatts.
Sentinel Data Centers wants to put four buildings on 160 acres of farmland there, in unincorporated Lake County, for $5 billion.
Indiana has four working data centers drawing 931 megawatts between them, and 36 more proposed, which would come to nearly 16 gigawatts.
Lake County sits on the seam between the MISO and PJM grids, in a region built on steel and oil refining that has been losing both since the 2000s.
Much of the argument here is about the utility rather than the developer.

In September 2025 regulators approved a NIPSCO subsidiary, NIPSCO Generation LLC, which is exempt from the usual certificate of public convenience review, negotiates data center contracts confidentially, and has funded 2.6 gigawatts of combined cycle gas generation for Amazon projects.

Critics point out that the subsidiary and the utility share a parent company, NiSource, that ratepayers may still end up carrying grid maintenance costs, and that there are no standard contract minimums or clean energy requirements.

NIPSCO customers are facing a $77 a month increase per 1,000 kilowatt hours over two years, and in April 2026 the utility locked out 1,600 United Steelworkers members in a dispute over the use of nonunion contractors.
Ben Inskeep of the Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana said: "We've lost a lot of trust with NIPSCO," and described a large public outcry against the plan.
The opposition organised fast.

A Facebook group passed a thousand members within weeks of the announcement in January, and the campaign has run on yard signs, several Facebook pages and petitions, with dozens testifying at the February commission hearing and hundreds at a town hall in April.
One organiser said it "feels like a David and Goliath feat".

Residents raised water use by the air cooled chillers, noise, the loss of farmland, and the 1,423 adjoining acres held by Ceres Partners and recently acquired by WisdomTree, which has fed a suspicion that more will follow.

Randy Niemeyer, a Lake County councilmember who sits on the plan commission, described where his constituents start from: "The reason I think people are so skeptical and have pushed back with such fervor is because they've been lied to so many times." He added: "They've had a lot of things in areas like this over the years shoved down their throats."
He also said: "if we don't figure this out, somebody else is going to, and we're not going to have a seat at the table."
The dates run: a plan commission study session on 17 December 2025, a public hearing on 18 February 2026, a town hall on 16 April, and a further public hearing on 20 May 2026.
Sentinel postponed the rezoning vote after the February hearing.
The plan commission's vote is only advisory: the rezoning needs the Lake County Council, and the Board of Zoning Appeals then controls the final permit.

A website at projectshirleylakecounty.com acts as a clearing house for the process, listing those dates and acknowledging that a project of this scale raises legitimate questions about land use, electric infrastructure, water, environmental protection, agricultural character, property values, traffic and noise.
It does not name Sentinel, gives no acreage, megawatts, water figure or investment, and does not say who runs it.
The 877 megawatt R M Schahfer coal plant is 22 kilometres away, with two solar plants totalling 756 megawatts at 26 and 28.
Eight moratoriums and zoning limits are now in force within reach of the site.

unconfirmed: How the Lake County Plan Commission voted on 20 May 2026, and whether the county council has since considered the rezoning, are not established. No water figure has been published for the project. Sentinel is not quoted in anything read and appears to have made no public statement of its own. Who operates projectshirleylakecounty.com is not disclosed on the site, so whether it is the county's, the developer's or a third party's could not be determined. The archived Chicago Tribune report in our record was not fetched.

sentences.t: Metrobloks, a data center developer, filed on 16 October 2025 to rezone a nearly 14 acre lot on Sherman Avenue in the Martindale-Brightwood neighbourhood of Indianapolis, in Marion County, Indiana, for two data halls with a car park, generators and cooling plant.

The site at 2505 North Sherman is a vacant lot that was once a drive-in theatre, in a historically Black neighbourhood shaped by railroad expansion and lead smelting, whose contamination residents have spent years trying to clean up.
The campus is put at $500 million, and the Los Angeles company pledged $2.5 million towards affordable housing and infrastructure, rising towards $20 million depending on a tax abatement.
The Metropolitan Development Commission approved the rezoning on 1 April 2026.
Cierra Johnson, who organises with One Voice Martindale Brightwood, answered it: "What we are saying is that you cannot come into Martindale Brightwood and just do anything. We matter."
She added: "Our hope is still that they pack up their things and go home. We are going to continue to fight this thing."
The City-County Council gave final approval on 4 May 2026.

Councillor Jesse Brown tried to pull the rezoning from the agenda, which would have forced a public hearing before the council voted, but only the councillor for the affected district may make that request.
"There's no correct answer that will make everyone happy," Brown said afterwards. "Why would we not err on the side of just calling for a vote, which would then call for a public hearing?"
A non-binding resolution of his, urging the commission to stay approvals for high impact data centers, passed the same night.

The objection had always rested on the neighbourhood's own plan, as Johnson put it when the application was filed: "We would like to see development that is in alignment with our quality of life plan, which definitely has an environmental justice component, but also has wellness components."

On 1 May 2026 residents and the Hoosier Environmental Council filed for judicial review of the commission's decision, arguing that it "failed to properly apply variance standards" and that Metrobloks had not carried out adequate studies of environmental impact, water use, utility use and traffic.
Johnson, by then the group's president, said: "We feel as though we have been sidelined and that this has not been reviewed properly and that it may have been predetermined."

Metrobloks says the halls would draw power under contracts with AES Indiana rather than from the residential grid, and would cool on a closed loop filled once and recirculated, taking about 19,000 gallons for the first building and about 47,500 for the second.
The company argues that is less water than the warehouses or light manufacturing already permitted under the site's industrial zoning.

Alejandro Maldonado, a co-founder of Metrobloks, said: "The parcel in question has served in the past as a truck facility and railyard, and we seek to build a modern, sustainable data center on this parcel."

City-county councillor Ron Gibson, who represents the area, supports the project and says it differs from the larger campuses proposed elsewhere in the region; in April his home was shot at, a note reading "No Data Centers" was left behind, and nobody has been arrested.
Residents called a meeting at Polk Stables for the evening of 12 May 2026 to go through the complaint and what came next.

unconfirmed: No megawatt figure or water demand for the finished campus appears in anything read, and no square footage could be sourced: outlets that would not open are reported to give roughly 168,000 square feet and 36 generators, and the Metropolitan Development Commission's vote as 6 to 2 on a written ballot, so none of those figures is used above. The Indianapolis Recorder returns 403 to both a plain request and a browser one, and the WTHR report in the record returns 403. The record's status of under construction is not supported: the approvals are zoning approvals, and nothing read says work has begun. Whether the judicial review has been decided was not established. Searches this pass: 'Metrobloks Martindale-Brightwood Indianapolis data center rezoning Metropolitan Development Commission decision'.

sentences.t: Lifeline Data Centers, a colocation company, runs its Indianapolis data center from the building it calls Eastgate, at 401 North Shadeland Avenue in Marion County.

The company bought the 40 acre former Eastgate shopping center in May 2008 from JTL Capital of Dallas, and in 2011 the City-County Council voted 23 to 6 to lease 76,000 square feet of it for 25 years as a public safety complex, at $685,000 a year for the first ten years.

Lifeline says the site is powered by a 4 megawatt solar farm at the facility, backed up by IPL's coal fired power fed from more than one substation, and offers security "anything from FISMA, to Top Secret".

In 2016 it said it had 120,000 square feet across its Indianapolis sites, and its owners, Rich Banta and Alex Carroll, were then shielding a new $17.5 million data center in Fort Wayne against electromagnetic pulse.

Lifeline also used to rent space in the downtown carrier hotel at 733 West Henry Street, and in July 2022 it told customers it would leave at the end of the year because the new owner, Netrality, was raising its rent by 300 percent; its other two Indiana data centers were at 401 North Shadeland Avenue and in Fort Wayne.
Netrality answered that the lease had run "for over 15 years without any escalation in the rental rate" and in January 2023 bought Lifeline's colocation business there.
Southwest of the corner of Washington Street and Shadeland Avenue, on a former Ford factory site near Irvington Community Elementary School, DC Blox has proposed a $2 billion data center campus.
The Metropolitan Development Commission approved it on 15 July 2026, and on 14 August neighbors and Irvington Community Schools went to court for a judicial review.
A month later, on 19 August 2026, the same commission voted 6 to 0 for a moratorium on new data centers in Indianapolis through 2027.

unconfirmed: The record's single source, a Data Center Dynamics report of January 2023, concerns Netrality's purchase of Lifeline's colocation business at 733 West Henry Street in the Indy Telcom Center, not the 401 North Shadeland Avenue building the record locates; the July 2022 report confirms Lifeline separately operates at 401 North Shadeland. The record's description of this site as acquired by Netrality appears to conflate the two. No capacity, floor area or date for the Shadeland data center itself was found beyond the company's own claims; the Indianapolis Business Journal report on the 2011 lease was read only as reposted on Lifeline's website, and the 2016 figure of 120,000 square feet may cover both the Shadeland and West Henry sites. Searches this pass: 'Lifeline Data Centers Eastgate 401 North Shadeland Indianapolis expansion 2026'. It returned only colocation listing sites and aggregators, which give 210,000 square feet, an Uptime Tier IV Gold certification, tornado-resistant reinforced concrete and 23 networks on site; none of that is used above because none of it is a source this page would cite, and Lifeline's own locations page carries no specifications at all. No news report, resident comment, complaint or hearing about this building was found, and there appears to be none.

sentences.t: DC Blox, a data center developer from Georgia, won city approval on 15 July 2026 for a $2 billion campus in the Thunderbird Commerce Center, the old Ford plant site near Irvington on the east side of Indianapolis, in Marion County.
The approved plan at 305 Fintail Drive is smaller than the one first filed: a one story, 70,000 square foot building due in two years and a two story, 250,000 square foot building in five.
The Ford Visteon plant opened on the site in 1957, made car parts until 2007 and was demolished in 2017, and Lauth Group and Covington Group bought the land in 2021 for an industrial park.

DC Blox filed in April 2026 for three buildings of 80,000, 140,000 and 190,000 square feet, and Bill Thomson, its vice president of marketing, described the cooling: "Rather than continuously pulling from utility water, we'll fill up our water system one time from the utility, and then we continue to recirculate the water within the system."

The land is zoned heavy industrial but Indianapolis has no zoning class for data centers, so the company asked for a variance of use, which the Metropolitan Development Commission decides and the City-County Council cannot call down.

At a Warren Township meeting on 21 May 2026 some residents held signs reading "Block DC Blox", and Julie Watson said that "these meetings happen, and then regardless of how the residents feel, the data center goes in anyway."
The company's David Armistead answered: "Not all data center companies are the same, and not all data centers are the same."
On 11 June 2026 the commission's hearing examiner, Judy Weerts Hall, recommended approval.

Residents shouted "Shame on you"; Dawn Briggs said "promises are not the same as proven facts, and assurances are not the same as enforceable commitments"; and Councilor Andy Nielsen cited his own survey in which 83 percent of respondents opposed the campus, while Councilor Michael-Paul Hart, whose district shares the site, held off.

DC Blox then published 20 commitments: to pay all utility costs and enroll in AES's green power program, use closed loop cooling, draw no groundwater, test generators only outside school hours, and give at least $20,000 a year for five years to the Pennsy Trail.
Mikey Hess, a lifelong east sider, said: "I just don't trust it at all."

On 9 July 2026 the company cut the plan from three buildings to two, from 56 diesel generators to 31 and from about 80 megawatts of demand by 28 megawatts, moving the buildings toward the middle of the park, away from the trail and Irvington Community Elementary School.
The commission approved it 6 to 1 a week later.

Heather Rodriguez, who chairs the Irvington Community Schools board, told it: "What they are really asking for, a permanent change to what this land may be used for, next to an elementary school, is a rezoning dressed up as a variance."

On 14 August 2026 two neighbors, Irvington Community Schools and Eastside Community Action filed for judicial review in Marion Superior Court 5 and asked for construction to be halted while it is heard.
Megan Lapa, a plaintiff who lives near the site, said the objections raised on 15 July were "disregarded so pretty carelessly".

The school, with about 300 pupils, is 850 feet from the site according to the lawsuit, and the conditions require vapor mitigation, a two foot soil barrier on open ground, and a sound study showing no more than 65 decibels at the campus edge.
Rachel Maldonado, the charter network's chief executive, visited a DC Blox center in Atlanta and heard a generator from 700 feet away, and said: "We're only getting a snapshot."

The city's moratorium on new data centers, passed by the development commission 6 to 0 on 19 August 2026 and running through 2027, does not reach this campus, and DC Blox is also pursuing tax abatements.

unconfirmed: The record lists 100 megawatts and $2.2 billion; DC Blox gave 80 to 100 megawatts and up to $2.2 billion in its original filing, WFYI reported up to 78 megawatts, the July 2026 cut removed 28 megawatts, and DCD reports $1.8 to $2 billion for the approved plan. Permanent job figures conflict: 35 in the April plan, 17 in Mirror Indy's July 9 report and 21 in its July 15 report. The record lists the project as under construction; the reporting says the first building is planned within two years and does not confirm that work has started. The Irvington school details come from a Chalkbeat Indiana story republished by Mirror Indy. The three DCD sources in the record now open with a browser user-agent and were read in full. Searches followed Mirror Indy's DC Blox tag page and WFYI's related coverage; the change.org petition "Reject the DC Blox data center and protect Irvington's future" was not read.

sentences.t: US Signal runs a data center it calls IN02 at 6325 Morenci Trail on the northwest side of Indianapolis, in Marion County.
The company bought the single story, 9,600 square foot, 2 megawatt building in December 2023 as its second data center in Indianapolis.
It had been the only site of Rack Bunker, a local colocation firm founded in 2019, and before that was used by the disaster recovery company BlueLock, which InterVision bought in 2018.

US Signal said it bought the building and land from the previous ownership group, not Rack Bunker's business, and planned 300 cabinets once upgrades were done, with room on the several acres for up to 600 more as demand allowed.
The upgrades were managed by Etzel Engineer and Build, ran more than six miles of new fibre out to over 500 enterprise locations, and added ten to twelve jobs.
The building was cut open to visitors on 11 July 2024 and opened that August, with customers buying cabinet space before it did.
Chief operating officer John White said the site was "another step in our five-year plan to build additional digital infrastructure in our Midwest footprint."
US Signal, founded in 2001 with its own 9,500 mile fiber network, had itself been bought earlier that year by Igneo Infrastructure Partners.

The company now lists the building as built in 1975 and updated in 1984, 2006, 2010 and 2024, with 2,500 kilowatts of generators, 1,600 kilowatts of UPS, a 2,500 kVA utility feed, 500 tons of cooling and six carriers on site.
It pairs the building with IN01, its space in a downtown carrier hotel, for customers who want a second site in the same city.

On 10 August 2026 the City-County Council voted 23 to 1 to stop new data centers in Indianapolis through the end of 2027 while it writes rules on sound levels and on plans for water and electrical capacity.

Council President Maggie Lewis said the pause would give councilors time to fine-tune those rules, and the lone vote against came from Councilor Michael-Paul Hart, who said: "If we had development standards in place, you could always pick a more restrictive set of commitments."

unconfirmed: The record lists no capacity; Data Center Dynamics reports 2 megawatts and 9,600 square feet at purchase, and US Signal's own page gives equipment ratings but no total floor area or critical load. Listings that would not open are reported to give 1.6 megawatts and a Tier III rating, so neither figure is used. Whether the Indianapolis moratorium would cover an expansion at an existing site, such as the 600 extra cabinets US Signal said it might add, is not addressed in the reporting on the vote. Searches this pass: '"US Signal" Indianapolis data center 2026 expansion Morenci Trail IN02'. Nothing beyond the company's own releases, Data Center Dynamics and colocation listing sites carries this building: no local news report, resident comment, complaint or hearing about it was found, and there appears to be none.

sentences.t: Prologis asked Kosciusko County, Indiana to rezone more than 500 acres of farmland near Leesburg from agricultural to industrial so that a data center could be built on it.

The land, on the north side of CR 700N west of CR 300W in Prairie and Jefferson townships, belongs to Tim Polk, Polk Family Farms and Murphy Place LLC, and adjoins a NIPSCO substation on a 20 acre tract.
The county said no twice.

The area plan commission heard comment on 2 April 2025 and recommended refusal, with about 350 people watching online, roughly 100 more in an overflow annex, and more than a thousand signatures gathered against the proposal.
On 22 April 2025 the commissioners upheld that recommendation 3 to 0, before 114 people in an old courtroom that holds 120.
Commissioner Bob Conley gave three reasons for the motion: the citizens had spoken, the plan commission had spoken, and now the commissioners were speaking.

Commissioner Sue Ann Mitchell said she supported data centers in logical locations and had met Prologis in person, and concluded that "the rezoning of property should be denied because it is not a reasonable and prudent location for this type of development".

Commissioner Cary Groninger said he had visited five data centers in Indiana and Illinois and met commissioners in St Joseph and Allen counties, and that the limitations of this location "have not been overcome by the petitioner".

Attorney Steve Snyder had put the petitioners' case on the land itself: "We have the convergence of three 345,000 watt transmission lines on these parcels, and that is what is essential to what is being proposed."
He offered a voluntary condition restricting the rezoned ground to a data center and nothing else, and said $10 billion would go into ten buildings, each carrying 30 jobs paying over $100,000.

JC Witt, Prologis's data centers vice president, said the site was chosen because it was the least disruptive way to reach power the county already has, and that if it were refused "it's not going in another location".
Water use, construction routing and off site improvements, Witt said, were things the company would address later in partnership with the county.

Attorney Jack Birch, for the objectors, answered that the voluntary condition bound nothing else and that power lines can be moved or extended: "We're not against a data center. We're against a data center in this location."

Residents came in neon hats reading "No data center", and Lisa Hay, Gary Parker and Craig Charlton spoke about the ground: "We're gonna lose over 500 acres of really good farmland and there's a lot of homes up there."
They said it would change how people live there, the Amish farmers among them.

Randy Warren, the agriculture teacher at Wawasee High School, argued for protecting prime farmland, and Courtney Van Cleave asked the commissioners for a one year moratorium while data centers were researched.
Afterwards Chris Polk said the decision told Warsaw's businesses that "Kosciusko County is closed for business", and worried aloud about the orthopaedic companies that had wanted the project.

unconfirmed: The commission's own vote on 2 April 2025 is reported by the Times-Union as an 8 to 0 recommendation and by WSBT without a count or a named commissioner. The record's acreage of 550 sits against "over 500 acres" in both reports and 535 acres in Prologis's own explanation of why the parcel is larger than the buildings; the $10 billion in the record is confirmed as the petitioners' figure. The earlier version of this page rendered the transmission lines as "three 45,000 transmission power bolt transmission lines" from WSBT's garbled quotation; the Times-Union gives Snyder's words as three 345,000 watt lines, which matches the 345 kV rating of the NIPSCO lines, and that is used above. A quotation from Christina Archer of the Leesburg town board carried by WSBT ("You were crying because it just is such an emotional thing for me") is not used because it does not parse. Whether Prologis appealed, refiled or went elsewhere after April 2025 was not established, and nothing published since names the end user. Searches this pass: 'Kosciusko County Leesburg Prologis data center 550 acres after denial 2026'.
